doc.title: Dick Griffin interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, February 12, 2024

chapter: Jackson, Medgar Evers and high school band
title: Lunches with Medgar Evers and Mr. Harriton's story
summary: Asked about Evers's assassination, Griffin recalls lunching with Evers for three years, his sister's sit-in, and Mr. Harriton who passed for white and freed Evers from jail.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: I’d like to jump forward a little bit, and this is a bit of a tangent but in 1963 I think you were 23, that was the year that Medgar Evers was assassinated. And I’m wondering, can you put into words how that affected you?

Well yeah. 1963 was the year that I graduated and got my bachelor’s degree. But prior to that I would eat lunch with Medgar Evers for three years from ’60 to ’63. There was a place called Smacko’s in Jackson on Nth Street. And Smacko’s was the place right across the street from Medgar Evers’ office, which was in the, we called it the State Office Building. And at lunchtime there were no fast food places, but people that didn’t go home for lunch went to cafes and they had home cooked meals there. And as a college student I lived in the city which is on the east side of town, and the college was on the west side of town, so when I came to school over on the west side I wasn’t going back home to eat lunch or anything because my mother was a domestic worker and she wasn’t even there to cook a meal. So we ate at this place called Smacko’s, it was every day for three years. © Fillius Jazz Archive -8-

And that was, oh a very devastating part of my life, you know he was killed because my youngest sister was in a meeting that night that he had organized the youth to go and do a sit-in down in the city in Jackson. Because the reason for that is my youngest sister was a teenager and I was an adult. I was 23 years old. Had I sit-in they would have sent me to the State penitentiary and booked me as a real criminal or something like that. But as a youth, teenagers, my sister, they could arrest them but they couldn’t keep them, not book them as any kind of crime or anything. So my sister, she did sit-in maybe one or two times. There would be so many students there they built a tent in the area down on the hill. They built a tent and they put all of them in the tent. And the parents would have to come and claim them, sign them out or come and get them. So my sister, she said — and I didn’t know that — they would just throw bread, a loaf of a bread and bologna in the tent — treated them like they were animals. And I never knew that until very late in my life, how they treated my sister. Because my mother picked them up and my sister, she never talked about how they treated her. But Medgar Evers was a very, very good friend in that he would sit and tell me about all the different ventures that he had going into these towns where he was arrested. And this is something that never was written and probably won’t be, but there was a guy named — I think his name was Robert Harriton. Mr. Harriton — he looked like white on sight. From two blocks away if you saw him coming you thought he was a white guy. And all his kids and his family. And we had a family like that. But Mr. Harriton and Medgar was very good friends. So when he got put in jail in a small town he would call Mr. Harriton. This was a real true story and hasn’t been written — probably nobody knows about it. So Mr. Harriton would go down, Mr. Harriton on his driver’s license had white, you know, on his driver’s license. So he would go down and basically get Medgar out of jail. And they would go in and said Mr. Harriton this thing [inaudible] all right you’ve got my boy ba-ba-ba in jail, and they said, “oh well you know he’s good,” and they would get him out of jail and they would drive — probably have Medgar be driving him and he’d be sitting in the back from habit. And once they got out of the city limits they would just laugh and say wow, you know. And when Medgar got killed the reason I know this story is I have a friend, Willie Salor, his wife was the daughter of Mr. Harriton. And Mr. Harriton, his son played in my band in high school. His name was Robert Harriton. We called him Booty. And Booty was a baritone saxophone player. And the reason that music has been so good to me, in high school I had a band and we would play proms for white high school, junior high school and everything. We’d play for the proms. Because there was no canned music and everything, all music for the proms and graduation and everything was live music. 1950s, ’57 and all of that — so we were playing this gig and Robert Harriton looked like a white guy. Nothing — hair, complexion and everything. So, and we were playing this junior © Fillius Jazz Archive -9-
